extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers of science interested in foundations of biology and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for judging biological concepts (especially whether life can be treated mechanically) and for giving a scientific definition of 'life' without falling into metaphysical projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of a biological concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Any biological concept will be scientifically valid if it enables us to briefly summarize without internal contradiction any range of our perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of a biological conception rests on its power to resume facts into brief formulae; scientific concepts are judged by their descriptive power and internal consistency rather than by metaphysical claims. (See also the stated aim of describing the widest ranges of phenomena in the briefest possible formulae.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not project conceptual constructs into the phenomenal world (avoid metaphysics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment the biologist asserts that a concept is a reality of the phenomenal world, although no perceptual equivalent has yet been found for it, he at once passes from the solid ground of science to the quicksands of metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: treating 'gemmules', 'germ-plasm', 'atom', or 'molecule' as empirically real without perceptual evidence; such projection weakens scientific position. Conceptual models should be kept as descriptions unless perceptual equivalents are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism is conceptual shorthand, not explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is the description in conceptual shorthand (never the explanation) of the routine of our perceptual experience; life as a mechanism would be an economy of thought rather than an explanation of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanistic description may allow use of one shorthand instead of two (organic vs inorganic) but does not 'explain' life any more than gravitation explains a planet's path. Beware treating mechanical description as causal explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clarity when using physical concepts (matter, force) in biology
rubrics_metrics.description: When biological statements involve an appeal to the conception of force or matter, we must ask what individual thing is conceptualized as moving, what is the field with regard to which it is considered as moving, and how its motion is conceived to be measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biologists should be careful in borrowing physicists' language; specify the items being modeled (particles, fields, measures) to avoid metaphysical vagueness. This is an operational test to reveal metaphysical clothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test hypothetical entities by their power to resume facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of a conception (e.g., gemmules, germ-plasm) can only be tested by the power it gives us of resuming the facts of heredity; lack of direct observation is not by itself a disproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analog: gemmules not being found doesn't disprove Darwin's conceptual hypothesis any more than failure to see atoms in the air disproves atomic theory. But projecting such conceptions as real without perceptual support is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use consciousness or metakinesis as defining marks of life
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot postulate consciousness as a means of classifying living and lifeless organisms; metakinesis (a putative pre-consciousness) is merely a metaphysical name without perceptual description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciousness is only directly perceived in ourselves and is not a reliable empirical criterion across organisms; potentialities (like metakinesis) without outward recognition marks do not provide a scientific definition of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define life by secondary, observable characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Because life cannot be defined by a single sense-impression, we must define it by secondary characteristics: atomic/chemical structure (protoplasm of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen; proteins + water), characteristic modes of growth, cyclical reproduction/renewal, and specific environmental requirements (moisture, temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These secondary characteristics are the practical biological distinctions (e.g., inner growth vs crystal surface growth, reproduction cycles). They collectively mark off organic from inorganic phenomena though the distinction is ultimately described as a set of characteristics rather than a single essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before asserting mechanical description of life, determine whether organic motions obey the same physical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: One must determine whether the motions by which we conceptualize organic phenomena can be resumed in the same laws as those for inorganic phenomena; current mathematical analysis may not suffice to deduce organic laws from atomic laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The atomic/structural complexity of organic corpuscles makes synthesis of their motions difficult; even if organic motions were ultimately reducible to atomic laws, that would not remove the mystery of life, and presently we cannot assert deduction of one from the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of scientific description: brevity and wide applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The object in biology (as in physics) is to describe the widest ranges of phenomena in the briefest possible formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological aim favors conceptual economy; however, economy of description should not be conflated with ontological claims about unseen substrata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical axiom: omne vivum e vivo
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as present experience goes, there is no generation of living from lifeless substance; the routine is from living to lifeless (death) but not from lifeless to living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom bears on debates about spontaneous generation; claims to the contrary require empirical demonstration rather than metaphysical inference from decomposition processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attribute self-determination to simplest organisms without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of self-determination as an attribute of living organisms likely arises from very complex systems; it is doubtful that elementary organic corpuscles possess any power of self-determination beyond motion determined by environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign 'self-determination' only where observations (e.g., stored sense-impressions leading to behavior) justify it; avoid ascribing autonomous agency to primitive life-forms without empirical basis.
